If you don't already have a stash of primers, you're probably better off foraging for factory ammo then trying to reload a stockpile right now. I could go find a couple of boxes of 9mm right now, but small pistol primers are long gone.

Also, reloading defense loads is not for everyone. Sure, you could just go yeet a bunch of range brass through a progressive press and get some decent plinking ammo, but if you are loading for defense, you really need to treat every single cartridge like your life depends not only on that cartridge going bang and cycling your weapon, but on also going where you aimed it. You need to chamfer and clean the primer pocket on every single case. Also, if you shoot the 10mm derived cartridges (10mm, 40 s&w and 357 sig), you probably need to at least check the case length on every single case. That goes without saying with rifle cartridges.

I use brand new brass for my EDC loads, and match headstamps on everything else.

When you work up new loads, don't just go shoot a ladder test, call it a day, and go load 1000 of them. Do the ladder, set your load, then load at least 150 rds of that load. Then go to the range and shoot those 150 rds in a variety of ways. Do a mag dump or two, drop a full mag, then shoot it, chamber then eject a few without firing them, then shoot them. Basically stress test those 150 RDS, and if you get through all of them without a malfunction, then go home and load 1000s of them. Also make sure every once in awhile you grab a box or two from your stash and make sure they still function correctly.

If you're willing to take the time and spend the money, you can definitely load ammo that is more reliable, more accurate and more powerful then even the boutique factory ammo, but it takes patience and the desire to do so.

This is old shit to people who have been reloading awhile, but judging from the shelves at my local reloading stores, there's a lot of new reloaders out there who probably haven't learned this shit yet.
